rationale: A wins because it gives the founder the missing earnings-quality spine: "Peloton Says It's Profitable. The Balance Sheet Tells a More Complicated Story." That is the story any serious business desk will test first, and A turns it into a real financial angle with GAAP loss, debt maturity, exclusions, and free cash flow as proof. B is disciplined, but "Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike" writes a causal comparison the facts do not support. Useful set, but one headline is borrowing credibility from evidence it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash" is sloppy chronology and not supplied in the update; the pandemic made Peloton famous before the crash narrative took over.
"The Target Customer Is Not Who Bought One in 2020" assumes a changed buyer before rental-cohort data exists. A flags the proof need, but the headline still overclaims.

"Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash" and "What Keeps 6 Million Peloton Subscribers Paying" both lean on churn, loyalty, and the same 6 million member fact. They are close cousins; one needs sharper retention mechanics or they should merge.
The next step sends users to "meanest-editor" before locking the missing proof. For these angles, EBITDA/FCF figures, debt maturity, rental price, and CEO access come before pitch drafting.
gaps_in_B: "Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike" invents a comparison and implied causality. The update gives no new-bike data and no driver of churn.
"The company everyone wrote off" is a lazy universal. If the prevailing belief matters, show the coverage pattern; do not make "everyone" do the reporting.
B never makes the net-loss-and-debt skepticism its own angle. It buries the most obvious public-company story as a caveat inside other angles.
"after three years of losses" blurs adjusted EBITDA profitability, free cash flow, and net profitability. For a public company, that kind of mush gets you corrected fast.
